sections.title: Detailed Brief Overview
rows: What/Who
Evaluation of **Author Tone** and **Author Viewpoint** in UP Assistant Teacher English exam passages.
Core Focus
Identifying the emotional attitude, intent, and objective or subjective perspective of a writer.
Why Important
Carries high weightage in reading comprehension questions testing higher-order critical thinking.
Key Features
Differentiating between **objective**, **subjective**, **critical**, **satirical**, and **neutral** writing styles.
Sub-types/Major Works
Classifying tones into positive, negative, neutral, and humorous categories based on diction.
Significance for Exam
Direct questions asked on identifying author mood, intent, and underlying stance from short passages.
Linguistic Basis
Relying heavily on **lexical choices**, **syntax**, **modifiers**, and **connotative vocabulary**.
Evaluation Criterion
Testing candidate ability to look beyond literal meaning to interpret figurative and stylistic devices.

items.title: 1. Definition and Distinction: Tone vs. Viewpoint with **Mnemonic**
items.content:
• **Author Tone:** The emotional state, attitude, or mood of the writer towards the subject.
• **Author Viewpoint:** The ideological stance, opinion, or perspective the author holds on the topic.
• **Diction Indicator:** Tone is revealed through word choices (**connotation**), whereas Viewpoint is revealed through thesis statements and arguments.
• **Mnemonic:** **'T-V'** -> **T**one is **T**emperament (How they feel); **V**iewpoint is **V**antage point (What they believe).

items.title: 2. Classification of Tones: Positive and Negative Spectrum
items.content:
• **Positive Tones:** Optimistic, laudatory, enthusiastic, reverent, supportive, hopeful, and admiring.
• **Negative Tones:** Critical, pessimistic, cynical, sarcastic, scathing, hostile, and condemning.
• **Lexical Markers:** Positive tones use terms like 'breakthrough', 'pioneering'; negative tones use 'flawed', 'regrettable', 'ill-conceived'.

items.title: 3. Classification of Tones: Neutral and Analytical Spectrum
items.content:
• **Neutral Tones:** Objective, factual, detached, informative, educational, and unbiased.
• **Analytical Tones:** Critical, investigative, probing, logical, and methodical.
• **Stylistic Markers:** Absence of emotional adjectives, presence of statistical data, passive voice construction, and balanced reporting.

items.title: 4. Humor, Irony, and Satire in Author Stance
items.content:
• **Sarcastic/Satirical:** Mocking, ridiculing, using irony to expose human vice or folly.
• **Whimsical/Lighthearted:** Playful, fanciful, amusing, and non-serious.
• **Cynical:** Believing that people are motivated purely by self-interest; distrustful of human sincerity.

items.title: 5. Step-by-Step Method to Identify Tone in Exam Passages with **Mnemonic**
items.content:
• **Step 1:** Scan for **adjectives and adverbs** carrying emotional weight.
• **Step 2:** Look at the concluding sentence for a summary of intent.
• **Step 3:** Distinguish between the author's voice and quotes cited from others.
• **Mnemonic:** **'S-L-C'** -> **S**can adjectives, **L**ook at conclusions, **C**heck for quotes.

sections.title: Important Facts and Data
rows: Objective
Data, statistics, neutral verbs, absence of pronouns ('I', 'we')
To inform or report facts without personal bias
Subjective
First-person pronouns, emotional adjectives, personal anecdotes
To share personal experience or emotional perspective
Critical
Flawed, erroneous, misguided, failure, superficial
To point out weaknesses, errors, or negative aspects
Laudatory / Praise
Commendable, visionary, exceptional, remarkable, triumph
To praise, honor, or express admiration for a subject
Sarcastic / Ironical
Shocking discovery, brilliant idea (used contextually wrong)
To mock, ridicule, or state the opposite of literal meaning
Didactic
Must, should, duty, moral, instruction, guidance
To teach, preach, or impart a moral/ethical lesson
Apprehensive
Looming threat, uncertain future, worrying trend, fear
To express anxiety, dread, or doubt about future events
Nostalgic
Reminiscent, bygone era, golden days, bittersweet memory
To express sentimental longing for the past

items.definition: Strip away the nouns and verbs from a sentence and look solely at the **adjectives**. If the adjectives are purely descriptive ('large', 'green', 'historical'), the tone is **neutral/objective**. If they are evaluative ('atrocious', 'brilliant'), the tone is **subjective/biased**.
Ask whether the paragraph reads like a **hard news report** (objective tone) or an **editorial/opinion piece** (subjective, persuasive, or critical tone).
Rank words on a scale of -5 (extremely negative/hostile) to +5 (extremely positive/laudatory). The cluster of words chosen by the author determines the exact quadrant of the **tone matrix**.
Watch out for **exaggerated praise** in contexts where failure is evident; this immediately flags the tone as **sarcastic** or **satirical** rather than laudatory.
Identify modal verbs like **should**, **must**, and **ought to** which instantly signal a **didactic** or **persuasive** author viewpoint.
Remember that words like **'assert'** and **'argue'** indicate an opinion-based viewpoint, whereas **'state'** and **'report'** indicate an objective viewpoint.

items.term: Mistake 1: Confusing Author Tone with Passage Topic
items.definition: Students often pick the topic as the tone. **Tone is the attitude**, not the subject matter. A passage about a disaster can have a **scientific/objective** tone, not necessarily a panicked one.

items.term: Mistake 2: Assuming Quoted Opinions are the Author's
items.definition: Authors frequently quote critics or opponents to refute them. Always check whether the author agrees with the quote or is setting up a **counter-argument**.
A neutral tone is not a lack of quality; it is a deliberate stylistic choice reflecting **detachment and impartiality**, common in academic and scientific texts.
Do not label a passage **'scathing'** or **'hostile'** if the author uses mild corrective feedback like 'needs improvement'. Match the intensity of the vocabulary to the tone option.

items.term: Mistake 5: Confusing Objective Reporting with Sympathy
items.definition: Describing human suffering objectively does not mean the author's tone is 'sympathetic'. Look for explicitly empathetic diction before marking a tone as **compassionate**.
Transitions like **'however'**, **'nevertheless'**, and **'on the other hand'** often signal a shift in the author's argument or tone. Never judge tone solely from the first sentence.
The writer's emotional positioning and attitude toward the subject matter, conveyed through **diction** and **syntax**.
The underlying belief, philosophy, or ideological stance held by the writer regarding the passage's central theme.
Unbiased, factual, devoid of first-person pronouns, relying entirely on **verifiable evidence** and data.
Personal, emotionally charged, reflecting individual experiences, opinions, and feelings.
Characterized by fault-finding vocabulary, analytical breakdown of flaws, and skeptical questioning.
Characterized by high praise, admiration, celebratory adjectives, and respectful phrasing.
Sarcasm uses verbal irony for mockery, while cynicism reflects a broader distrust of human motives and goodness.
Designed specifically to teach moral lessons, instruct readers, or guide ethical behavior.
Words carry secondary emotional meanings; decoding **connotative power** is key to finding the exact tone.
Always cross-verify tone options against the concluding paragraph and recurring **evaluative adjectives**.

upscNotes.content: For UP Assistant Teacher exam comprehension questions on tone, eliminate extreme options first (e.g., 'furious', 'hateful', 'adoring') unless the passage text features exceptionally intense vocabulary.

Examiners often place a trap option that reflects a character's tone in a story rather than the author's overall tone. Always distinguish between a character's spoken dialogue and the author's overarching perspective.
When asked about the author's viewpoint, look for thesis sentences usually located in the opening paragraph or the concluding summary paragraph of the reading passage.
Do not let your own personal opinion on the passage topic influence your tone selection. Base your answer strictly on the lexical evidence provided in the text.

keyTakeaways: Author tone reflects emotion and attitude; author viewpoint reflects belief and stance.
Objective tones use facts and neutral language; subjective tones use personal pronouns and emotional modifiers.
Diction and connotation are the most reliable indicators for deciphering subtle tones like irony, skepticism, or cynicism.
Didactic texts aim to instruct, whereas analytical texts aim to investigate and explain.
Transition words like 'however' and 'yet' frequently indicate shifts in the author's line of reasoning or emotional stance.
Always eliminate extreme options in tone questions unless backed by strong, unambiguous textual evidence.
